source.title: You Only Cache Once: Decoder-Decoder Architectures for Language Models
source.authors: Yutao Sun; Li Dong; Yi Zhu; Shao-Han Huang; Wen-Hui Wang; Shu-Ming Ma; Quanlu Zhang; Jian-Yong Wang; Fu-Ru Wei

record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation loss across model sizes and fits scaling curves, using the same basic size-versus-language-modeling-loss measurement as the original claim, on YOCO and Transformer variants.
record.gate_note: Section 4.2 and Figure 4 report validation loss across model sizes. Section 4.2 says curves were fitted but gives no numeric fitted exponents or explicit test of small-run predictions on larger runs. Appendix Table 8 reports separate validation perplexity results, including fine-grained subsets. Downstream-task scores, long-context results, and inference-cost results do not test the listed scaling versions.
record.test_reason: Section 4.2 and Figure 4 plot validation loss against parameter count (160M–13B) for Transformer and two YOCO variants, and the authors say they fit scaling curves as in Kaplan et al. This is the original V1 measurement, though it serves an architecture comparison and gives no exponents. Tokens are fixed at 10B.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that YOCO matches Transformer language-modeling performance while cutting inference memory and prefill latency by orders of magnitude. The scaling claims (competitive scaling from 160M to 13B, YOCOgRet best) support that architecture argument rather than testing scaling laws themselves.
record.recipe_differences: Uses validation loss across parameter counts and fits scaling curves, but tests YOCO architectures (gated retention and sliding-window attention) alongside an optimized Transformer under this study's training setup; it does not reproduce the original studies' full parameter, token, and compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture choice affects comparative loss: the paper reports YOCOgRet outperforming Transformer and YOCOSWA; the Appendix G.1 AR-Hit results show larger architecture differences than the overall validation-set results.

fits_no_version.finding: At 160M parameters, architecture families differ in validation perplexity: Transformer 3.564, Mamba 3.645, RetNet 3.633, YOCOgRet 3.530. Gaps are larger on associative-recall tokens (AR-Hit: Transformer 1.219, Mamba 1.555).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, the choice of sequence-mixing architecture family changes loss modestly overall but substantially on recall-dependent tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: Cumulative NLL decreases with context length up to 1M on book and code data, and the authors say the curves tend to fit a power law (Figure 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss falls as a power law in context length.

record.problems: Figure 4 supplies no exact loss values in the text, and the paper reports no numerical fitted exponents or uncertainty for the scaling curves. The sweep holds training tokens at 10B and does not test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation.

untested.parts: Scaling in tokens or compute; fitted exponents; regime where data is not the bottleneck (tokens fixed at 10B up to 13B parameters).
All. The authors say the law is 'supposed to extrapolate' but do not test it.
All. Depth and width are never varied at fixed parameter count.
All. Downstream scores at 1T and 1.6T tokens are not related to scale or loss.

record.verdict_notes: This is an architecture paper, and its scaling evidence is thin: figure-only values, no exponents, and a 10B-token budget that likely bottlenecks the largest models. The reader's V4 linkage was wrong, because comparing architecture families is not the shape variation V4 describes.

versions.untested_parts: The study sweeps parameter count, not training tokens or compute, and does not report fitted exponents.
No explicit comparison tests whether a fit on smaller runs predicts larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is reported.
The study compares architecture families at matched parameter counts, but does not independently vary depth, width, or other architecture details while holding the rest fixed.
The reported scaling experiments concern language-model pretraining, not other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Downstream benchmark scores are reported, but the study does not test their predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not test sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup or fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.

relationships.condition: Transformer, YOCOSWA and YOCOgRet, 160M–13B parameters, 10B training tokens, figure-level evidence
relationships.reason: Figure 4: loss falls steadily with size and authors report curves fit as in Kaplan et al. No exponents or point values are given. Rows r01–r21.
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased steadily across 160M–13B parameters for Transformer, YOCOSWA and YOCOgRet, with reported Kaplan-style curve fits.
